answers.question: What is the app and stack?
answers.answer: B2B dashboard app, React front end, Node API, Postgres on AWS RDS.

answers.question: How bad is it and since when?
answers.answer: Customers say pages take 4 to 6 seconds. API p95 went from about 400 ms to 1.8 s over the last six weeks (Datadog, reported). Six releases in that time.

answers.question: What can your AI reach?
answers.answer: Datadog and GitHub, both read-only. Deploys use GitHub Actions and every production deploy needs the tech lead's approval.

answers.question: What counts as fixed, by when?
answers.answer: p95 under 500 ms within a month, with no downtime.

answers.question: Where do notes go and who decides?
answers.answer: Notes in the repo. The tech lead decides.

research.approach: Practitioners treat a latency regression as a comparison problem first. They tag every metric and trace with the release version, compare p95 per endpoint for matched windows before and after each deploy, and only then go down a level: which queries cost the most in total time (pg_stat_statements), what their plans look like (EXPLAIN with buffers, on a copy), and how much of the user-visible time is in the browser rather than the API. Fixes go in one at a time, each with a before and after number, and a latency guard is added so the same regression is caught on the next deploy.

steps.name: Pull latency by endpoint and release for matched windows
steps.why: A regression is only visible against the period before it, per endpoint and per version, not as one global p95.

steps.name: Check the comparison is like for like
steps.why: Traffic mix, time of day, cold caches after a deploy and sampling can fake or hide a shift.

steps.name: Attribute the slowdown to releases, endpoints and layers
steps.why: Compare each release with the one before to see which endpoints moved and whether time is in code, queries or the browser.

steps.name: Rank queries by total time and read their plans
steps.why: Total time weighs how slow a query is by how often it runs; plans show scans, repeated nested loops and stale statistics.

steps.name: Separate browser time from API time
steps.why: Customers feel 4 to 6 seconds; the API p95 is only part of that. Each layer needs its own fix.

steps.name: Fix one cause at a time and measure before and after
steps.why: One change per fix keeps the gain attributable and each fix easy to roll back.

steps.name: Add a latency guard for future deploys
steps.why: A per-route p95 check after each deploy catches the next regression in minutes, not six releases later.

steps.name: Deploy gradually with version tags and watch
steps.why: The owner needs each deploy approved and no downtime; a tagged, watched, reversible deploy gives that.

pitfalls.text: Reading averages or one global p95: a stable mean can hide a tail that doubled, and a shift on one route disappears in the total.
Comparing a peak-hour deploy with off-peak data, or reading numbers in the first minutes after a deploy while caches are cold.
Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production writes: it executes the statement. Use a replica, a copy or read-only statements.
Assuming a changed plan is a regression, or an unchanged plan is fine: data growth can slow an identical plan.
Fixing the API while the browser is the larger share of the 4 to 6 seconds.

If the target was missed, the next hypotheses and the data needed are named

hypotheses.statement: A release added per-row queries (N+1) or extra queries on list and dashboard endpoints.
hypotheses.test: Compare database queries per request for the same endpoint across versions in traces, and read the diff of each release for new loops that query.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Queries per request rose on the slow endpoints at the release that added the loop.
hypotheses.refute_if: Queries per request are flat across versions.

hypotheses.statement: A query plan changed or data growth made a query scan too much: a missing index, or stale statistics.
hypotheses.test: Rank pg_stat_statements by total time, then run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a copy and compare scans, rows read and estimated versus actual rows.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Top queries show sequential scans, heavy buffer reads or large estimate gaps that match the slow endpoints.
hypotheses.refute_if: Top queries use sensible index plans and their time per call is unchanged.

hypotheses.statement: Responses got larger or less filtered, so serialization and transfer time grew in both API and browser.
hypotheses.test: Compare response size and API span time per endpoint by version; read the diffs for removed pagination or added fields.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Payload size grew by release in step with latency.

hypotheses.statement: Part of the 4 to 6 seconds is in the browser: bundle growth or re-rendering added by recent releases.
hypotheses.test: Build each release tag, compare bundle size, and profile the slowest pages; use real-user data if Datadog holds it.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Bundle or render time grew across releases on the slow pages.
hypotheses.refute_if: Browser time is flat and the API accounts for the full gap.

hypotheses.statement: The database or connection pool is short of capacity (CPU, IO or connections), not a code change.
hypotheses.test: Check RDS CPU, IOPS, connections and wait events and the app pool settings against the slow periods, if Datadog holds them.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Resource saturation lines up with the slow periods.
hypotheses.refute_if: Resources have headroom during the slow periods.

hypotheses.statement: Part of the apparent rise comes from the measurement: traffic mix, sampling or a version-tag change.
hypotheses.test: Re-read p95 on matched hours and volumes and check sampling and tags over the six weeks.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The rise shrinks a lot on matched data.
hypotheses.refute_if: The rise holds on matched data.

measurement.window: At least one full week of normal traffic after the last fix is live; compare the same hours and endpoints as the baseline.
measurement.min_volume: Enough requests per endpoint for a stable p95 in each matched window; if an endpoint has too few, report it as INCONCLUSIVE.
measurement.stop_rule: Stop and roll back a deploy if its p95 or error rate gets worse than the version before it after the watch window; otherwise keep the one-fix-at-a-time order.
